exports.1: We keep a man on the district heating network whose whole job is to walk the streets before dawn with a steel rod against the pavement and name which pipe is complaining; he has not been wrong since 2004 and he is desperately bored. Lend him a fortnight and he either finds your hum or he certifies it as nobody's, on letterhead, with a stamp — which is the second-best outcome and much cheaper.
exports.2: Don't argue with them, make them park there. Move one unavoidable event — the swim meet, the Christmas market, the vote count — physically into the district for a season, and let four thousand people be pleasantly surprised against their will; we'll send the two staff who ran that operation here for six years, because being wrongly written off is the thing we are genuinely best at.
exports.3: Signal back. We can send a serviceable lamp, a keeper willing to sit three nights, and the form — two long, one short, meaning received, no action required — and then it gets minuted and filed like anything else; we once bent a road four metres around a party that does not legally exist, and the paperwork we invented for it is still the calmest document in our archive. Nothing polite ever escalates once it has been answered in writing.
exports.7: We have geothermal heat we cannot switch off and eleven hundred square metres of glasshouse sitting empty above it until October. Put the plums on lorries by Thursday and you get them back nine days later as forty tonnes of dark fruit leather in wax paper, keeps two years, and we'll take the split ones as payment.
exports.8: Stop fighting it end to end and split it instead. We can spare forty angled glass baffles that came off our arcade when it was reglazed — set them staggered, knee to shoulder height, alternating sides down the whole run, and the avenue keeps its wind but loses the run-up, which is the part that takes the awnings.
exports.9: Put a queue on the far side. Licence renewals, passport photographs, the tax window — and one genuinely excellent bakery beside it, so the crossing is resented for about four months and then defended in public by people who claim they always liked the walk.
exports.10: The residents aren't wrong, they're just gambling every time they set off. We'll pay for the boards on all four approaches: live count of free spaces, and underneath it — this is the part that actually works — the number that were free at this hour yesterday, and the day before. People will accept a full car park; what they can't stand is not knowing before they leave the house.
exports.11: Stop planting trees on the front line. Take six hundred rooted cuttings of the salt rose that has colonised our own shore embankment — hideous for two years, an impassable four-foot hedge by year four, hips you can boil into jam — and put your trees in behind it in year five, where they will live.
exports.13: Take us. We have thirty years of documented experience being the team a bigger neighbour declines to consider a fixture, and we can supply the entire apparatus: a chant with one word in it, a coach who says the wrong thing to a reporter deliberately, and a grievance dating to a document signed in a wet field that nobody on either side has read.
exports.14: When our own hall was reroofed we kept the eleven trusses that came out — laminated timber, twenty-two metres, stacked in a heated shed doing nothing but staying dry. They're yours for the cost of the lorries, and we'll send the engineer who signed them off originally, who is retired, sharp, and would dearly love to be permanent about something.
exports.15: Dark rye, baked overnight in the ground where the heat is free, sliced an inch thick with cold butter, a boiled egg and a mug of fish broth. We'll send the two women who do it, the recipe, and the only rule that matters: no menu, no seating plan, lights kept low, and nobody at the counter asks how your night was.

answers.1: The northern lights. Half the town drives out to stand in a freezing ditch and comes back altered; I have looked up, seen green, said "yes, green," and gone in for my supper.
answers.2: The pool. Not the swimming — the hot tubs, in order, hottest last, where four hours is exactly long enough to learn everything worth knowing about this place from men who will tell you for free. Everyone assumes I'll drive them straight to the capital instead. It's eight minutes on the bus, they can manage that themselves later.
answers.3: Not "charming." I want somebody to say the buses were on time in a tone that makes it clear they expected nothing else.
answers.5: My original application form, where I had written the name of the town next door in the box, and the extremely kind letter that came back explaining it was taken. Let some future archivist work out how I felt about it, because I'm still not sure.
answers.7: Pool at half seven, when it's the same eleven regulars and the water is too hot for anyone in a hurry. Home by nine, something with potatoes, and then the specific pleasure of sitting at the kitchen window watching the glow over the capital where the loud thing is happening without me. My wife reads. I do the crossword badly and stop halfway. Nothing arrives, nobody rings, and at eleven the last bus goes past the end of the road and I go to bed.
answers.8: Not my predecessor, God rest him. The woman who has run the front desk at the pool since 1989 — she knows every name in this town and exactly how much complaint each one is worth, and she taught me to let people finish talking before I start being useful.
answers.9: My mother, who will listen to all of it and then ask whether it was in the capital's paper or only in ours.
answers.10: Next door, obviously. I have had my eye on it since the beginning. I'd want it noted in the record that I'd be arriving as a resident and not as a claimant.
answers.11: A snow globe of the cathedral next door, given to me by the office staff in my first week as a joke. I've left it there so long that moving it now would be admitting something.
answers.12: Whichever one I can undo in a year without anybody needing to be blamed.
answers.14: The plant room under the sports hall. It's warm, it hums at a pitch that makes conversation pointless, and in nine years the only person who has ever come looking for me down there was the caretaker, who now doesn't.
answers.15: The three descending tones the bus makes when it kneels at the kerb. Undignified, entirely reliable, slightly too slow.
answers.16: A brass key to the old boiler room door, which was bricked up in 2004. I keep meaning to have it cut off the ring and I keep not doing it.
